paper_title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires a method that can understand, generate, reason, and act across diverse domains and modalities. Rather than relying on a single model to master every capability, a promising path toward AGI now is to orchestrate a heterogeneous ecosystem of specialized models, tools, and policies (candidates) into a unified AI system. At the heart of this vision lies a fundamental question: how can an AI system dynamically select and coordinate the most capable candidate for each task while balancing performance and computational cost? In this work, we present Route Anything, a unified framework for studying model and policy routing across general-purpose AI systems. We develop a unified theoretical foundation that characterizes optimal routing under quality--cost trade-offs and establishes how the information available to a router determines its attainable performance. To systematically investigate routing across diverse capabilities, we first construct an omni-modal trajectory matrix spanning 25 benchmarks across language understanding, image, video, and speech generation, coding and workplace agents, and robotic manipulation, comprising 374,401 scored runs from 452 candidate configurations. Building on this framework, we train and test different routers to investigate the potential of omni-modal model routing, the capabilities of learned routers, and the conditions under which routing improves efficiency. Our results reveal substantial opportunities for capability orchestration: per-input oracle routing outperforms the best fixed candidate by 5.4 points, and learned routers outperform it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks, by 2.1 points on video generation, and by 1.1 points on robot manipulation while using 24% less policy time. More importantly, routing raises efficiency by 8.82x on average compared with the reference model.

sections.content: 31 2 Route Anything: Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems 1. Introduction Agentic AI systems now can draw on multiple kinds of specialized models, tools, and policies: language model answers question, an image or video generator renders prompt, speech model reads text aloud, and learned policy controls robot. Rather than relying on one model to master every capability, general-purpose system can orchestrate this heterogeneous ecosystem and choose, for each input, which module handles it. We call each such model, tool, or policy candidate. The best candidate changes from input to input, so router that chooses well is expected to match one fixed strongest candidate at fraction of its price, or beat it by sending every input to the most suitable candidate that handles it best. Routing research has mostly studied language models: cascades that escalate to stronger model [1], routers learned from preferences [2], and qualitycost formulations that connect the two [3]. Whether routing helps across modalities remains an open question. Thus we present unified framework Route Anything for studying model and policy routing across modalities. To support such anlyasitical framework, we first build an omni-modal trajectory matrix in which every candidate in pool runs on the same inputs, for 25 benchmarks across text and image understanding, image, video, and speech generation, code and workplace agents, and robot manipulation, with three to seven candidates per pool and 374,401 scored runs of 452 candidate configurations (Figure 1). We train and test routers using different strategies and ask three questions: how much can routing gain, how well do learned routers work, and when is cheaper route good enough? Our unified routing theory frames all three: routers value is the best expected outcome, net of priced cost, given what it observes, so what it can reach is ladder from the best fixed candidate to the per-input oracle, and reference policy with quality tolerance fixes the price of quality. The matrix measures each rung, and two code and text testbeds with recorded prices [4, 5] add the cost side. We also provide empirical insights through extensive experiments:

Inputs are split 70/10/20 into training, development, and test sets by source group, so identical inputs and items from one source never cross splits; RoboTwins 2,000 test scenes come from 10 tasks the routers never see in training. Finding 6: cheaper route is often good enough. Across the four testbeds of Table 5, routing raises efficiency over the reference by 8.82 on average (the mean of 25.5, 7.1, 1.35, and 1.33, with image generation at 𝜖 = 0.5). On CodeRouterBench, the admission price of Opus 4.6 is 𝜆 𝐵 = 100 score per dollar (2.9 𝜂𝐵), below the zero-loss floor price of 144 and far below 𝜂 = 1022, so by Corollary 6 the zeroloss router never calls Opus. It dispatches every task to cheaper model and reaches 25.5 Opuss efficiency at 0.44point loss  (Table 5)  . Always calling Qwen3-Max, the cheapest model, already reaches 20.1 at 4.2-point loss; routing by state recovers that loss while adding 27% efficiency. The states need not be oracle labels: prompt-inferred cells reach 25.3, and learned qualitycost routers 22.724.2 at their zero-loss points (Appendix C.2). Without states, every zero-loss policy calls Opus, which then runs on 28.7% of tasks. On RouterBench, the best router that avoids the reference scores 9.7 points below it, so the zero-loss router cascades cheap primaries to the reference and reaches 7.1. fitted floor is not guarantee. Refitted on half of the probing tasks, the zero-loss floor holds on test in only 12.5% of 200 splits; certified on the other half by Proposition 5 with empirical-Bernstein 𝑝-values on the mixture-refined path, it holds in all 200, at median 19.4. Image generation follows the same logic. GPT Image 2.5 costs $0.21 per image, 3.55.4 the other generators, and is the best candidate on two of the five benchmarks. The route that stays within half point on training prompts moves Qwen-Image-Bench to Grok Imagine 2.0 and OneIG to Qwen-Image 3, cutting test cost by 26% at 0.47-point loss, and two-point tolerance halves cost. In speech generation the best generator is also among the cheapest, so there is nothing to trade, and on robots the time saving of Section 4.2 comes with no loss of success. Router overhead is small next to these prices: 4B router takes 0.13s per decision on one H20 GPU, whereas generating an image takes 27158s and video 211314s. 5.2. Spending More Within Task Setup. candidate can spend more inside task: plan that retries after failure, or that verifies an output and escalates on rejection. router can also buy finer state: forecast of candidates success, or record of past outcomes. By Theorem 2, richer candidate is worth playing only if its value net of its full cost beats the candidates it replaces, and that value must be computed on the inputs that reach each step (Proposition 8). By Proposition 3, finer state can only help an optimal router, but it is worth buying only if the help exceeds its price (Proposition 9). We test both on CodeRouterBench, with fresh model calls for verifier verdicts and forecasts, and semi-synthetic streams for memory (Appendix C). Route Anything: Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems Finding 7: richer candidates and finer states are worth their cost only if they beat what they replace. Retries. failure leaves harder tasks: in all 42 ordered model pairs, the second model succeeds less often after the first fails (median ratio 0.49 at 𝜃 = 1). Verifiers. For Qwen3-Max at 𝜃 = 0.5, free compiler gate gives 4.09 dollar efficiency at 2.4-point loss, and an LLM judge 2.63 if free but 0.30 at its list price; in seconds, always-Opus beats every verified cascade, because Opus answers faster than the primaries. Finer states. forecast can save at most the attempt it replaces: DeepSeek-v4-pro forecast costs 2.4 attempts at list price, prompt-only TF-IDF router 0.06% of one. 6. Related Work Routing language models. Cascades and routers trade quality against cost [13], and learned routers estimate each models quality from the query [3438]. The acceptance step of cascade is reject option [39], studied as confidence-based or budgeted deferral [4044]. Dekoninck et al. [3] characterize optimal routing and cascading through Lagrangian price tuned to budget; here, the reference and the quality tolerance fix that price, and finite-sample test certifies the resulting floor. Routing benchmarks record per-model outcomes and costs on shared prompts [4, 5]. Routing beyond text. SCOPE-Router arranges vision-language models for execution-oriented tasks [19], and routing ideas also inspire vision-token pruning strategies [45], dynamic submodels for video segmentation [46], and acceleration policies inside diffusion transformers [47]. Coordinators, harness-level routers, and token-level routers extend routing beyond model identity [4852]. We study routing across output types on one matrix: language models, image, video, and speech generators, and robot policies, all scored on shared inputs. Portfolios and tools. Algorithm portfolios choose among complementary solvers per instance [53 55]. Their virtual best solver corresponds to our per-input oracle, and its advantage over the single best solver gives the potential gain in Proposition 3. Residual coverage measures what an additional solver contributes to the portfolio [56, 57]. Accounting for call costs connects this selection problem to fractional programming, which optimizes ratio objectives such as quality per unit cost [6, 58]. The value of information addresses the related question of whether acquiring routing signal is worth its cost [59, 60]. Similar cost considerations arise in test-time compute, where gains from extra calls depend on the task and allocation [61, 62], while imperfect verifiers can limit the gains from resampling [63]. Feedback-driven self-repair uses earlier attempts to guide later ones [64, 65], making resampling at equal cost natural baseline [66]. 7. Conclusion Across text, images, video, speech, code, and robots, the best candidate changes from input to input, and the per-input oracle sits 5.4 points above the best fixed candidate per benchmark. Most of that potential gain lies within task types, and learned type router already scores 0.3 points above the best fixed candidate across 16 benchmarks, and up to 2.1 points within an output group. In embodied scenarios, router trained on camera frames tracks the best VLA policy in each scene condition and beats the best single policy by 1.1 points with 24% less policy time. Routings most reliable gain is cheaper route that is good enough, raising efficiency over the reference by 8.82 on average: when candidates are close in quality and far apart in cost, the reference and the quality tolerance fix the price, and finite-sample test certifies the quality floor. Three rules follow: (1) compare candidates on the same inputs, and measure gains against the matched best fixed candidate; (2) train routers on per-candidate outcomes, and look for gains within task types; (3) fix the reference and the tolerance before ranking routes, and certify the floor on independent inputs. 12 Route Anything: Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems

Classical routers have negative native capture because their 𝑍 = 0 tasks still satisfy ℙ( 𝐻 = 1 𝑍 = 0) > 𝑎/𝑏 = 0.043, so withholding the attempt forgoes profitable ones. For the LLM forecast, DeepSeek-v4-pro reads the prompt and predicts whether Qwen3-Max and Kimi-K2.5 pass all hidden tests on 600 probing and 600 test tasks; its calibrated posterior reaches test AUROC 0.541 and 0.618 and capture of 0.037 [0.225, 0.077], and at list price it costs more than the attempt it could save in 22 of 24 states. 30 Route Anything: Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems C.6. Router Memory This semi-synthetic study combines real outputs and verifier judgments with constructed arrivals and retention: 2,044 probing and 867 test tasks in 12 cells. With probability 0.25 the writer explores uniformly sampled model, and it writes the models identity to the arriving cell when verification accepts; the newest record serves later tasks in that cell, and uncovered cells use the prior, always-Opus or the probing-fitted DimensionBest, which sends each dimension to its best model. Writers use ACRouters doctest and syntax tools, locally executed hidden tests, or DeepSeek-v4-pro judge; we report hidden-test writes. write is erroneous when the accepted output is incorrect under the released score; against that truth, hidden-test writes have TPR/FPR 0.960/0.205. Fifty streams of 60,000 rounds are measured over their last 10,000 rounds. With no expiration, the store reaches 135.8 score per dollar but scores 0.034 below always-Opus and 0.116 below DimensionBest. D. Limitations The theory takes the law of states as given, so it does not cover states that depend on the routers own earlier choices, such as SciCode steps that contain models earlier code, and certification needs the references outcome on every certification input. Moreover, step-level routing for long-horizon agentic tasks is more complex and deserves deeper exploration.
